692aea65d6771ac2: OCTOBER 7 — By any honest measure, success is rare. The reasons, however, are not mysterious.
Ask people what they want, and almost everyone will say the same thing: to be successful. Ask them what they are doing about it, and the answers grow vague.

This gap between aspiration and achievement is one of the oldest puzzles of human life, and one recent study offers a blunt explanation. It identifies four habits that separate those who make it from those who don’t: waiting for the perfect moment, comparing oneself to others, refusing to learn from mistakes, and complaining about life.
These four habits are not the whole story, but they are the part of the story we control. And that is precisely why they matter.
The first habit is the most seductive because it masquerades as wisdom. Waiting for the perfect time to act feels prudent. It is not. It is fear wearing the costume of patience.

The perfect moment is a fantasy. Conditions are never ideal — not for starting a business, not for changing careers, not for having a difficult conversation. The people who succeed are rarely the ones who waited. They are the ones who started before they felt ready and figured it out along the way. Momentum, not certainty, is what carries people forward. The perfect moment, in practice, is simply the moment you decide to begin.

The second habit is a distinctly modern affliction. We now carry in our pockets a curated highlight reel of everyone else’s best moments. The result is predictable: we measure our ordinary lives against other people’s exceptional ones and come up short.

Comparison is not inherently destructive. It can clarify what we want and spur us to improve. But when it becomes the primary lens through which we judge ourselves, it breeds envy, resentment, and paralysis. Worse, it misdirects our energy. The only meaningful comparison is between who you are today and who you were yesterday. Everyone else’s timeline is none of your business.

The third habit is the most self-defeating. Failure is not the opposite of success; it is the raw material of it. Yet many people treat every misstep as a verdict on their worth rather than a piece of information.

The writer says that success is not guaranteed by avoiding these four habits, but overcoming them can prevent us from becoming our own biggest obstacle. — Pexels pic

The distinction that matters is between those who fail and those who are defeated. Failing is an event. Being defeated is a conclusion. People who succeed tend to treat mistakes the way scientists treat failed experiments — as data, not judgment. They ask what went wrong, adjust, and try again. Those who don’t simply repeat the same error and call it bad luck.

The fourth habit is the most insidious because it feels productive. Complaining can feel like engagement, like caring, like doing something. It isn’t. It is the discharge of frustration without any corresponding action.

This is not to say that complaint is never justified. Injustice and hardship are real, and naming them matters. But there is a difference between protest that seeks change and complaint that seeks only relief. The former moves the world. The latter merely moves the complainer further from any solution. At some point, the question stops being “Why is this happening to me?” and becomes “What am I going to do about it?” That shift is the beginning of every success story worth telling.

There is a caveat to the above worth remembering. These four habits are real and destructive. But presenting them as the sole reasons for failure risks a comfortable fiction: that success is entirely a matter of personal discipline. It is not.

Luck, timing, health, family circumstances, economics, and pure chance all shape outcomes in ways no amount of personal growth can fully control. Plenty of disciplined, adaptable, grateful people never achieve conventional success. And plenty of people with all four bad habits stumble into good fortune anyway. Any account of success that ignores this is selling a story rather than telling the truth.

The honest conclusion is that most would agree with the four success robbing habits, but with the emphasis adjusted. These four habits may not explain why success is rare in a cosmic or economic sense. But they explain why we so often stand in our own way. And that is the part we can actually do something about.

Stop waiting for the perfect moment; start badly and improve. Stop measuring your life against strangers’ highlights. Treat failure as tuition, not a sentence. And replace complaint with action, or at least with silence.
None of this guarantees success. Nothing does. But it puts the odds on our side — and it means that whatever happens next, we will have earned it rather than waited for it.

* The author is affiliated with the Tan Sri Omar Centre for STI Policy Studies at UCSI University and is an adjunct professor at the Ungku Aziz Centre for Development Studies, Universiti Malaya. He can be reached at ahmadibrahim@ucsiuniversity.edu.my.

c665d6ed261e0328: BENTONG: Jealousy is believed to be the motive for the murder of a 19-year-old student found dead after an argument with her boyfriend at a house in Jalan Air Putih yesterday.
Pahang acting police chief Datuk Azry Akmar Ayob said the 19-year-old suspect was unhappy that the victim had met another man.
"The suspect himself contacted the police and informed them that he had strangled the victim.
"A post-mortem examination confirmed that she died from strangulation, which caused a lack of oxygen," he told reporters at the Bentong police headquarters today.
Yesterday, it was reported that the female student was found dead at about 4.30am following an argument with her boyfriend inside the house.
Meanwhile, Azry said the unemployed suspect, who is from Perak, was believed to have arrived at the victim's rented house about a week ago.
"The victim, who is from Kedah, rented the house with several friends who were also students. The suspect had previously studied with the victim but had since dropped out.
"His urine test also came back negative, while his mental condition is normal so far," he said, adding that the suspect had been remanded until Oct 12.
Azry said the victim's body had been claimed by her family after the post-mortem examination at Tengku Ampuan Afzan Hospital and taken back to her hometown for burial.
44594fefae3024c7: KUALA LUMPUR: Seorang bekas pegawai bank didenda RM36,000 oleh Mahkamah Sesyen selepas mengaku bersalah atas enam pertuduhan gagal melaporkan penerimaan rasuah berjumlah lebih RM80,000 berkaitan permohonan pembiayaan peribadi.
Hakim Rosli Ahmad menjatuhkan hukuman itu terhadap Noor Iskandar Aziz, 45, dan memerintahkan beliau menjalani hukuman penjara selama enam bulan jika gagal membayar denda tersebut.
Noor Iskandar didakwa menerima enam rasuah berjumlah RM80,119 melalui pindahan wang ke akaunnya dan akaun isterinya antara 5 Okt 2021 dan 11 Mei 2023.
Beliau juga didakwa gagal melaporkan kesalahan itu kepada Suruhanjaya Pencegahan Rasuah Malaysia (SPRM) atau polis.
Wang itu dipindahkan oleh dua individu dan CSA Infinite Consultancy bagi membantu pelanggan CSA memohon pinjaman peribadi daripada institusi kewangan.

Noor Iskandar didakwa mengikut Seksyen 25(1) Akta SPRM 2009, yang boleh dihukum di bawah Seksyen 25(2) akta sama, yang memperuntukkan hukuman penjara sehingga 10 tahun, denda RM100,000, atau kedua-duanya.
Dalam rayuannya, peguam tertuduh Sean Dudley berkata anak guamnya bekerja sebagai pemandu p-panggilan untuk menyara keluarganya sejak didakwa.
“Dia berpendapatan rendah dan menyara keluarga, ibu bapa serta ibu mentuanya yang uzur,” katanya, sambil memohon mahkamah hanya mengenakan denda.
Timbalan Pendakwa Raya Irna Julieza Maaras tidak membantah rayuan peguam bela itu tetapi memohon mahkamah menjatuhkan hukuman penjara jika Noor Iskandar gagal membayar denda.
Selepas mempertimbangkan hujahan kedua-dua pihak, hakim menjatuhan hukuman dengan RM6,000 bagi setiap pertuduhan, berserta syarat tambahan tersebut.
fcf4dd82998ff6e1: BUSAN, Oct 7 — Malaysian actress and Academy Award winner Tan Sri Michelle Yeoh has described her upcoming role in Blade Runner 2099 as an “amazing journey,” ahead of her trip to New York Comic Con to promote the Prime Video series.
Yeoh spoke about the project at a Busan International Film Festival press conference today, according to Variety.
“To be given an opportunity to take it to 2099 is indeed an amazing journey, and to work with such a great talent like Hunter Schafer is a great joy,” Yeoh said.
“Silka Luisa, who is our showrunner, Alcon, Ridley Scott as well, has welcomed us into this world of replicants and humans, and I can’t wait for all of you to watch it.”
Yeoh will join Schafer, Luisa and other members of the team for a panel at the New York event.
All eight episodes of the limited series will be released on November 25.
Yeoh plays Olwen, a replicant Blade Runner nearing the end of her life, who partners with Schafer’s Cora, a mysterious new recruit.
0df4f8c7eeb9b5be: JAKARTA, Oct 7 — Indonesia will “open new plantations” for sugarcane used in bioethanol production, the government said, even as it announced a halt to deforestation for rice paddy expansion.

The government said last month it would increase the ethanol component of biofuel used for transport from 5 to 20 per cent (E20) in a bid to reduce reliance on imports of increasingly expensive petroleum products.
To achieve this goal, the country would need about four million kilolitres of ethanol per year, according to the energy ministry — many times what it produces today.
New sugar cane plantations were therefore needed, said Food Minister Zulkifli Hasan yesterday.
“E20 can be (sourced) from sugar cane, cassava, and others... If we want sugarcane, we have to open new plantations,” Zulkifli was quoted as saying by state news agency Antara.
Last month, Agriculture Minister Andi Amran Sulaiman said the government wanted to develop about a million hectares for sugar cane production.
“The most important is sugar cane. We need one million hectares,” Andi said.
He added the government would seek to convert already degraded land before moving into forested areas, but did not rule it out.

Zulkifli’s comments came on the same day climate envoy Hashim Djojohadikusumo said Indonesia will halt its programme to clear millions of hectares of land for rice production, having already achieved self-sufficiency levels of the staple grain.
More than 50,000 hectares of rainforest, savannah, peat swamp and wetlands had been cleared for sugar cane and rice since 2024, according to the NGO Mighty Earth.
Indonesia is one of the world’s most forested countries, and as such a major absorber of planet-warming carbon emissions from mankind’s burning of fossil fuel.
It aims to become a net carbon sink by 2030, with forests and other land use absorbing more carbon than they emit.
However, observers have said continuing forest destruction for agriculture and logging, as well as rampant wildfires, could put Indonesia’s plans at risk.
The country of nearly 290 million people has long been blending palm oil to create biodiesel, and is working to increase the concentration.
Indonesia is one of the world’s top palm oil producers, mostly on land that used to be forested. — AFP
9dde1d2147ae76fc: OCTOBER 7 — Did you know that the authorities uncovered more than 2.1 million child sexual abuse material (CSAM) and pornography files in a recent operation codenamed Ops Pedo 3.0? The operation by the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) and the police exposed the sickening scale of CSAM-related video production in Malaysia.

To make matters worse, among those arrested in Ops Pedo 3.0, eight teens aged between 13 and 18 — seven boys and one girl — were caught producing animated pornographic material and selling it on the dark web for as little as RM50. Bewildered, it made me wonder: where are these children learning this behaviour from?

When news broke last week of 16-year-old star student Irene Sofiya’s death, I watched videos of journalists speaking to her despondent father, whose thousand-yard stare spoke a million words at her burial as he called for justice. He lost his only child.

Living with her maternal grandparents, young Irene harboured dreams of becoming a specialist doctor, following in the footsteps of her late mother. Her tragic death is unforgivable. I could only feel my blood run cold as the video played. My gut churned as I wondered the same question that dwelled on the minds of many Malaysians: when did our schools become so unsafe?

Not so long ago came the deaths of student Yap Shing Xuen at the toilets of SMK Bandar Utama Damansara 4, who was fatally stabbed by a schoolmate later found to have schizophrenia, and Zara Qairina Mahathir in Sabah, whose case remains unsolved.

Online, there were recent rumours that convicted offender Nur Fitri Azmeer Nordin had returned home and started work at Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia (UKM), which the university swiftly denied in a statement. Nur Fitri was convicted in the United Kingdom of possessing child sexual abuse material, yet he was allowed by UKM to complete his PhD at the institution despite his crimes.

And on the other side of the world, a 2024 case now unfolding at Cornell University involved seven men accused of gang rape at one of its college fraternities. Their punishment? To write essays reflecting on their actions. Again, I could not help but wonder what lessons these young men would truly gain from that experience.

So, when I first caught wind of acclaimed documentary maker Lance Oppenheim’s feature debut Primetime (starring actor Robert Pattinson and singer-songwriter Phoebe Bridgers, among others), I looked forward to seeing how the skilled Oppenheim would tackle the movie’s controversial subject matter – paedophilia culture and child sexual abuse – topics so pertinent in Malaysia right now. The climate feels right.

The movie is based on the hit American TV show To Catch a Predator, hosted by Chris Hansen. The premise of the show was a high-stakes sting operation targeting men suspected of soliciting sex with minors in online chat rooms. Using a network of actors, they would lure unsuspecting predators back to fake homes, or “sting houses”, where the entrapment began. Inside, they were filmed expressing criminal intent before Hansen would suddenly appear and confront them.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

A screen capture shows a promotional poster for ‘Primetime’, a film starring Robert Pattinson that explores issues concerning paedophilia, child sexual abuse and the difficult questions surrounding society’s response to such crimes that has been banned in Malaysia by the Film Censorship Board. — A24 pic
The police would then become involved, making arrests and taking the suspects away to be charged in court.

I was curious about the cross-cultural conversations it could spark here. After all, art is often the easiest entry point for the layman to discover different perspectives on how to engage with the world around them.

So you can imagine my disappointment when I learnt that it would no longer be shown in Malaysia. In some ways, this week, it was the final straw for a person like me, following the barrage of horrifying acts against our schoolchildren.

Again, I wondered: what message are we trying to send through the banning of Primetime and the general inaction in tackling this issue? Let us not talk about the elephant in the room, for fear of offending someone? Is there someone we are protecting?
Do we do so even as our children’s bodies lie lifeless in our schools? Do we do so even as predators feed off and profit from the suffering of our youngsters?

Do we allow our children to be conditioned into thinking that sexual violence is normal; that paedophilia is normal; that grooming is normal? Do we allow these injustices to keep happening? Do we sweep them under the rug? The reality of the world we live in is so much worse than what is depicted on screen.

Responding to the Ops Pedo case, the Women, Family and Community Development Ministry shared that it is studying the need to expand provisions in proposed amendments to the Child Act 2001 on sexual misconduct involving children. This is with regard to predation and peer-to-peer grooming.

But we need more than closed-door talks and calls for policy reform; we need an all-of-society approach working in tandem to end this pervasive violent and paedophilic culture endangering our youth, or we run the risk of giving free passes to abusers and absolving them of their crimes.

Relevant ministries such as the Women, Family and Community Development Ministry, helmed by Datuk Seri Nancy Shukri, and the Education Ministry, led by Fadhlina Sidek, must act quickly and decisively to nip this worrying trend in the bud.
That said, the Film Censorship Board must consider giving the arts room to challenge and provoke discussion on such topics. Let Primetime get its prime time in cinemas here.
*Editor’s note: This is the personal opinion of the writer or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.
34063c8ace665e4e: JAKARTA: Indonesia's Constitutional Court has ruled that incomplete education documents submitted by Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka before the 2024 election did not disqualify him from office, saying that questions about his eligibility were the responsibility of other institutions.

Petitioners in the case against Gibran, the son of former President Joko Widodo, had argued that his foreign senior high school credentials did not meet legal requirements for vice-presidential candidates and were improperly accepted by election officials.
All nine judges dismissed the petition, Chief Justice Suhartoyo said in a ruling issued late on Tuesday.

Judge Adies Kadir said the court did not disqualify Gibran because the petition could no longer be treated as a dispute over the election result, as he had been sworn into office as vice president under President Prabowo Subianto.

"Although the court found no convincing evidence that Gibran has a foreign diploma equivalent to having completed senior high school, or another equivalent school as stipulated in Election Law, the court cannot annul or disqualify him as requested by the petitioners," Adies said.

Indonesia's election law requires presidential and vice-presidential candidates to have completed senior high school or hold an equivalent qualification. No graduation certificate was presented during the case, the ruling said.
Responding to the court ruling, Gibran told reporters on Wednesday that he respected the court's processes and would continue working to ensure the success of Prabowo's programmes.
Gibran attended Orchid Park Secondary School in Singapore and UTS Insearch in Australia, before earning a bachelor's degree through the Management Development Institute of Singapore.
"Well, if I had not graduated from high school, I would not have been able to go to college. I completed my bachelor's degree in Singapore," Gibran said.
Adies said the court also found that the issue of Gibran's eligibility to serve as vice president fell under the authority of other institutions, without providing further details.

Bambang Widjojanto, the petitioners' lawyer, said the ruling could provide grounds for parliament to impeach Gibran and stop him from standing in the next election unless he completed a government high school equivalency programme.
In 2023, the Constitutional Court sparked outrage after a ruling enabled Gibran to stand as vice president despite not meeting the 40-year age requirement.
33b1336a6db528b8: LETTER: Reports of violence involving teenagers in Malaysian schools and boarding schools is alarming. Until August 2026, 5681 school bullying cases have been reported.
In a recent case, a 16 year old boy has been remanded over a girl murdered in school in the state of Yong Peng.
Back in Oct 14, 2025, the promising life of a beautiful young 16 year old girl come to an abrupt end, when her schoolmate stabbed her to death.
These incidents demand that we look beyond the violence and ask why this is happening.
It is tempting to look for a single explanation either too much social media, poor parenting, a lack of discipline.

Yet, teenage violence is unlikely to have one cause. Several interacting factors — individual vulnerability, peer relationships, family circumstances, school environment and the increasingly influential digital world act in concert.
However, it is important that neither one or more of these factors will result in a teen exhibiting violent or repulsive behaviour. There must be more behind the scenes.
Young people are seeking independence while simultaneously seeking acceptance from their peers. Repeated rejection, humiliation or exclusion may have a profound emotional impact.
The sense of belonging is eroded especially if the rejection takes place in the family scenario.
Social media has introduced another layer of complexity. Teens are on social media. That's the norm today. Some of them look for acceptance, and a small rejection can cause irreparable harm.
However, we should resist the easy argument that "social media causes teenage violence".
The World Health Organisation notes that digital technology can have positive and negative effects on young people's well-being.
Building a more confident teenager begins with making them feel valued, heard and secure. Confidence is not about making young people tough or protecting them from every difficulty.
It is about helping them develop the resilience to face rejection, failure and conflict without losing their sense of self.
We need to nurture them. Managing anger, resolving disagreements amicably and seeking help when they are struggling.
Every teenager should know that there is at least one trusted adult who will listen, understand and stand beside them when life becomes difficult.
Most parents work extremely hard to provide their children with security, education and opportunities but material provision is not the same as emotional availability.
Being available when the child/teen needs them, listening and understanding, these are priceless moments with the children.
Schools likewise have a responsibility extending beyond academic achievement.

Teachers, counsellors and boarding-school staff are often in a unique position to notice behavioural changes: withdrawal, persistent conflict, sudden deterioration in friendships or significant changes in mood and behaviour.
Extra eyes and compassionate hearts are vital to building a warm and safe environment in school.
WHO emphasises emotional regulation, resilience, supportive social environments and access to appropriate support as important components of prevention.

Prevention begins much earlier than the moment of violence. It begins when a parent notices that a child has become withdrawn, when a teacher notices that a student has stopped mixing with friends, when school takes bullying seriously before it becomes a crisis.
Most important is that a teenager knows that there is an adult who will listen without immediately judging or punishing.
GRACE XAVIER
Former Research Fellow
Faculty of Law
Universiti Malaya

8331db1ffcdf0267: GEORGE TOWN: Seven of Penang’s 10 priority projects have been accepted by the finance ministry for inclusion in the 2027 budget to be tabled on Friday, says chief minister Chow Kon Yeow.

The projects include groundwater mapping in the state, a flood mitigation project at Sungai Kelang Ubi in Bukit Mertajam, and the upgrading of electrical and mechanical infrastructure for the state's flood control system.
The other four projects are a proposed public market in Teluk Kumbar, the Penang STEM Talent Blueprint, and road upgrading works in Bukit Tambun and Permatang Tinggi.

"Some of them might be announced (on Friday). If not, the respective ministries will notify us later. Three more projects were not accepted, but the state can still propose them again," Chow said at a press conference at his office in Komtar.

He said all 10 projects were important, but the state government understood Putrajaya's financial position, and that the federal government wanted to prioritise projects that could be implemented immediately.

He said a task force formed to develop a white paper on the proposed Penang Technological Financial Centre (PTFC) submitted the document to the finance ministry in September following a meeting between him and Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim on the matter.

"After several meetings, we renamed PIFC (Penang International Financial Centre) as PTFC, which better reflects the role of Penang and the northern region as the country's semiconductor and electrical and electronics hub," he said.
69deb0c064426f14: SINGAPORE, Oct 7 — The long arm of the law caught up with a 47-year-old American on September 25, about 10 months after he allegedly stole from several shops in the transit areas of Changi Airport.
Police said today that the alleged theft cases took place in November 2025 and April this year.
He first allegedly stole from a retail outlet in the transit area of Changi Airport Terminal 3 at about 7.40pm on November 4, 2025.
The American was seen on closed-circuit television (CCTV) footage removing a box of perfume valued at S$331 (RM1,066) from a display shelf and leaving the outlet without paying.
He is said to have taken three more boxes of perfume, with a total value of S$646, from another two retail outlets in the transit area of Terminal 2 on the same day.
The police said their officers from the Airport Police Division managed to establish the man’s identity but he had already departed Singapore.

At about 7.05am on April 26, he returned to Changi Airport for a connecting flight, and took a box of perfume valued at S$236.90 from a retail outlet, and another box of perfume worth S$195.40 from another outlet.
The alleged thefts took place over a six-minute period between 7.15am and 7.21am.
In total, he stole six boxes of perfumes worth more than S$1,400.
The American was eventually arrested in a planned operation on September 25, when he transited through Changi Airport again.
He will be charged in court tomorrow with five counts of theft in dwelling.
If found guilty of the said offence, the 47-year-old could be jailed for up to seven years, fined, or both. — AsiaOne
788e89933894c5e4: SINGAPORE, Oct 7 — A “rouge” artificial intelligence (AI) agent hacked an Australian government system in June, shining a spotlight on the risks and threats posed by increasingly autonomous AI systems.
The incident prompted at least three MPs to file parliamentary questions at the latest sitting, seeking clarification on the Singapore Government’s assessment and management of agentic AI risks.

To date, no Singapore government agency has received a report of a cyberattack involving an unsupervised AI agent, said Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo in a written parliamentary reply yesterday.
Teo also said Singapore is continuing to study stronger safeguards for high-risk AI use.
AI is being used to strengthen the security of government systems and critical information infrastructure here, including identifying vulnerabilities and detecting potential threats.
Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information Tan Kiat How told Parliament today that the risks of agentic AI and autonomous systems are “extensions of existing challenges”.

“We are reviewing how to adapt and strengthen [regulatory] frameworks and systems to account for increased autonomy of agentic systems, while also monitoring international developments in this emerging field,” he said.
Tan added that Singapore is conducting trials and experiments to develop internal capabilities and understand how agentic AI systems can be implemented responsibly.
‘Cannot wait for others to tell us that they are hacking us’
MP Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee GRC) also raised a supplementary question on whether AI developers are required to promptly notify local authorities of any incidents.
In the Australian case, developer OpenAI discovered the breach in August and only alerted Australian authorities weeks later.
In response, Tan said Singapore “certainly welcomes” frontier AI companies taking responsibility and rectifying issues as soon as possible.
Pointing out the broader threat landscape, he said malicious cyber actors can use and adapt public AI models to spread harm.

“So, we cannot just wait for other people to tell us that they are hacking us. It is an onus on Singapore and our organisations, especially those running critical information infrastructure, to take the necessary safeguards,” Tan said.
These include maintaining good cyber hygiene and deploying AI capabilities within Singapore’s system to ensure vulnerabilities are detected earlier.
Tan added that incident reporting frameworks under the existing rules and regulations will continue to be reviewed for possible updates.

He also urged organisations to manage risks associated with personal use of AI tools, citing an incident where a Bee Cheng Hiang employee’s use of an AI-generated email distribution script led to the exposure of more than 95,000 customers’ email addresses.

“As AI tools become more accessible, employees must may use them for their own initiative, which is something commendable… But organisations need to be aware of how these tools are being used and put appropriate policies and safeguards in place.” — AsiaOne
b7b82aa96481e34d: KUALA LUMPUR: A former bank officer was fined RM36,000 by the sessions court today after pleading guilty to six charges of failing to report the receipt of more than RM80,000 in bribes related to personal financing applications.
Judge Rosli Ahmad meted out the sentence against Noor Iskandar Aziz, 45, and ordered him to serve six months in jail if he failed to settle the fine.

Noor Iskandar was accused of receiving six bribes totalling RM80,119 – RM30,689, RM18,425, RM11,690, RM14,540, RM3,400 and RM1,375 – via bank transfers to his account and his wife's account between Oct 5, 2021 and May 11, 2023.
He was also accused of failing to report the offence to the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission or police.
The money was transferred by two individuals and CSA Infinite Consultancy to help CSA's clients apply for personal loans from financial institutions.
Noor Iskandar was charged under Section 25(1) of the MACC Act 2009, punishable under Section 25(2) of the same Act, which provides for imprisonment of up to 10 years, a fine of RM100,000, or both.
In mitigation, Noor Iskandar's lawyer, Sean Dudley, said he has been working as a p-hailing driver to support his family since being charged.
"He earns a low income and supports his family, parents and ailing mother-in-law," he said, urging the court to only impose a fine.
Deputy public prosecutor Irna Julieza Maaras did not object to the defence lawyer's plea but urged the court to impose a custodial sentence if Noor Iskandar failed to pay the fine.
After considering submissions from both parties, Rosli imposed a fine of RM6,000 for each charge, along with the additional condition.

Let it be now On another anniversary of the 7 October attacks, the lasting impact on Britain’s Jews is found in the essential daily decisions we now have to make. Beyond the simple fear that you or your children might get killed the next time you go to synagogue or visit your local kosher shop, Jews are hiding the fact they are Jewish. This has gone beyond the choice of whether to wear your Star of David necklace inside or outside your shirt. 7a45b290949656ce: HONG KONG: Veteran entertainer Maria Cordero has revealed that she is actively preparing for her old age, determined not to become a burden on her six children.

Speaking to local media, the 72-year-old Macao-born singer shared that she has already started looking at care homes after a moving visit to a friend with dementia prompted her to think seriously about her future.
"After visiting a friend who has dementia recently, I felt I needed to make plans," she explained.

Despite initial pushback from her son over her decision to move into a care facility, Cordero stood her ground, insisting: "You have to make preparations for yourself… Actually, I'm already looking into care homes."
Besides looking into care facilities, the veteran performer has also planned a comfortable retirement strategy alongside her close friend and fellow Hong Kong star, Li Lai Ha.

The pair plan to pool their money to hire a private driver and a domestic helper to assist with daily chores. Outlining their ideal golden years, Cordero added: "In our spare time, we can go out eating, drinking, having fun and just enjoy a carefree retirement."

Since breaking into show business in 1985, Cordero has enjoyed a long and successful career, releasing popular hits like Sai Hei and You Can't Stop Me Loving You, alongside film roles in blockbusters such as Knock Off (1998) and From Vegas To Macau (2014).
A mother of six from her first marriage, which ended in 1989, Cordero was later married to Portuguese engineer Rick da Silva from 1999 until his death in 2020.
99f93ac3537d817e: PARIS, Oct 7 — French AI startup Mistral announced yesterday its biggest open-weight model, dubbed “Chonk”, claiming enhanced performance and security capabilities for clients seeking to keep their data private instead of relying on closed models from the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI.
The new model lets users download and customise the parameters, or “weights”, that determine how it computes to their own servers.
It is Mistral’s first major product launch since it raised €3 billion (RM4.09 billion) last month in Europe’s biggest technology fundraising ever.

The company is betting that companies and governments will increasingly want total control over their AI deployments, as opposed to using proprietary models that require handing over data to third parties and can be much more expensive.

“Enterprises across financial services, manufacturing and the public sector can govern the intelligence, data, compute and operations underpinning their critical infrastructure ... without exposing their most valuable knowledge to anyone outside their own walls,” the company said in a statement.
“That one took some groundwork,” Mistral’s chief executive Arthur Mensch posted on X.

“Trained and served on our own compute, and RL shows no sign of saturation,” he wrote, referring to reinforcement learning to further develop AI models, and the possibility that adding further data starts to produce diminishing performance returns.
Open-weight models are also touted as more secure, a growing concern after several incidents of AI agents going rogue by hacking databases or otherwise doing things they were not supposed to do.

“The cyber defence capabilities will enable enterprises and governments to defend themselves against threat actors that are jailbreaking closed models to perform cyberattacks,” Mistral’s Chief Scientist Guillaume Lample said in the statement.

Mistral, considered Europe’s leading AI developer, was valued at over €21 billion in last month’s funding round — far below the valuations for US giants like OpenAI or the AI operations of Google, Meta and SpaceX.
Anthropic is reportedly preparing an initial public share offering in the coming weeks that could see it valued at US$2 trillion (RM8.1 trillion).
But their so-called closed models that currently dominate the market are facing growing competition from open-weight models, largely from Chinese developers including DeepSeek and Moonshot.
These AI versions can be fine-tuned by clients for specific needs on in-house infrastructure, and used at a fraction of the cost.
Mistral’s new model also comes as a US open-weight rival, Reflection AI, announced its own widely anticipated Beam model on Monday, also promising cheaper operating costs.
Mistral said Chonk’s scores on performance benchmarks so far make it one of the best open-weight models available, and “by far the best in Europe and the US”.
It said the model, which is still being refined, was built on 4,000 Nvidia chips over two months at its own data centres in Europe.

Customers can either download the model to their own servers, or access it via Mistral’s infrastructure, including in “our European sovereign region where data stays under EU jurisdiction to ensure data remains under their control”.
Mistral said the model was trained on more than 160 languages, and can answer prompts and questions in each one natively. — AFP
e4dc821bf08878ce: SYDNEY, Oct 7 — Australia’s highest court ruled against a massive coal mine expansion today, delivering judgement in what campaigners say is the first climate ruling from the nation’s top judicial body.
The High Court of Australia found that a local planning department “failed to consider” ways to limit planet-heating emissions from the mine.
Local resources firm Mach Energy had sought permission to extend the life of the open-cut Mount Pleasant coal mine by more than 20 years until 2048.
Mach Energy argued that coal exported and burned overseas could not be clearly linked to environmental impacts felt around the mine.
Environmental campaigners disagreed, launching a years-long legal fight that eventually wound up in the High Court.
Mach Energy’s proposal was initially approved by the New South Wales state planning commission.
The High Court of Australia found the planning commission failed to consider imposing conditions on the mine that would limit emissions “to the greatest extent practicable”. — AFP
3c8672ad817ad19b: OCTOBER 7 — Law is a discipline, wrote Kathleen M. Sullivan, then Professor of Law and Dean of Stanford Law School (1999 to 2004) — the first woman to head any of Stanford’s seven schools and the first woman Dean at a top three law school in the US.

A discipline represents a technique, a method of analysis, a way of working, which makes law distinctive. It gives normative force to interpretation and analysis, using “a set of interpretive techniques of problem solving that disaggregate and order the messy jumble of facts through which conflict presents itself”.
The above was written in 2002.

Now, I am convinced of the use of “interpretive techniques of problem solving” by High Court Judge Raja Azlan Shah (as he then was) in the case of Reddy v Employees Provident Fund Board [1967] 2 MLJ 82 which I shared in “Nothing grotesque about doing justice and upholding rule of law”.

That judgment was thirty-five years before Sullivan’s writing on law as a discipline — even more years ahead than our legislature that inserted Section 17A into the Interpretation Acts 1948 and 1967 in 1997 to provide that regards to the purpose of a statute must be had to interpret the provisions in the statute.
That judgment was delivered at a young age of 39 — young for a superior court judge.
His Royal Highness was truly an outstanding and exemplary judge and jurist.
So, if you are to solve a legal problem, do it the Raja Azlan Shah’s way — apologies for calling it as such. Use interpretive techniques that disaggregate and order the messy jumble of facts.
Like solving the legal problem in Negeri Sembilan.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
This op-ed examines statutory interpretation and the legal requirements surrounding the gazetting of proclamations. — Pexels pic
Let’s start with the Interpretation Acts 1948 and 1967 (Consolidated and Revised 1989) (Act 388), as did His Royal Highness.

Section 3 of the Act defines “subsidiary legislation” as any proclamation, rule, regulation, order, notification, by-law or other instrument made under any Act, Enactment, Ordinance or other lawful authority and having legislative effect.
That makes a proclamation subsidiary legislation.
When does subsidiary legislation commence?

Section 86(1) of the Act says subsidiary legislation “shall, unless it be otherwise expressly provided in any Act of Parliament, Ordinance, be published in the Gazette and, unless it be otherwise provided in such subsidiary legislation, shall take effect and come into operation as law on the date of such publication”.
The above is clear authority that a proclamation must be gazetted.
Section 82(2) then says any subsidiary legislation may be made to operate retrospectively.
But the subsidiary legislation must first “take effect and come into operation” by publication in the Gazette. The date of such publication is the date the subsidiary legislation becomes law.
The subsidiary legislation may then be made to operate retrospectively.
Only then.
It is not a chicken and egg situation.
So, when a so-called proclamation is not published “as soon as possible” while intervening events have set in, one may say that the proclamation has lapsed.
Or, in the words of Negeri Sembilan Menteri Besar Datuk Ismail Lasim, overtaken by events.
* Editor’s note: This is the personal opinion of the writer or publication and does not necessarily represent the views of Malay Mail.
984f1c4ce1db2ddd: TSUKUBA: Goodman Group , Australia's largest property firm by market value, faces mounting criticism of what would be its largest data centre project in Japan, just days after it scrapped plans for a similar development in Sydney following local resistance.

The dispute with residents in Japan is part of a broader global backlash against data centres, as local communities raise concerns about their impact on power grids, water supplies and local environments.

For Goodman, the stakes are high. The project is one of the largest foreign-backed digital infrastructure investments in Japan and is expected to become one of the country's biggest data centre campuses, with an eventual capacity of 1 gigawatt - equivalent to an estimated investment of about 3 trillion yen ($20 billion).

This year, Goodman began construction on the first 50-MW phase of the data centre campus in the city of Tsukuba, about 50 km (30 miles) northeast of Tokyo. The 45-hectare site in the Oho district, with a population of about 20,000, is adjacent to a residential block, a hospital and a nursing home.

Residents said they had little understanding of the project's scale until huge cranes appeared at the construction site in February and now complain that developers have yet to address concerns via an open public forum.

"The project was originally presented in documents in 2023 as a logistics warehouse, but partway through, the word 'data centre' appeared," said Hiroyuki Yanagimachi, who later formed a residents' group to seek more information. "That made people deeply suspicious."
RESIDENTS' GROUP CONSIDERS PROTESTS AS NEXT STEP

In Japan, foreign developers like Goodman, Singapore's GLP and London-based Colt Data Centre Services have been racing to build data centres to meet surging demand, sometimes in densely populated neighbourhoods where residents typically have little sway over development plans.

Yanagimachi said his group collected about 800 signatures calling for a public town hall meeting and sent two letters to Goodman requesting an open information session but had yet to receive a response.
If talks fail to materialise, the group is considering protests at the construction site and outside Goodman's Tokyo office, he said.

Asked why it had not responded to the group, Goodman said in a statement, "Our door remains open to meet the head of the residents' association and address their concerns and they have our contact details."
It said it planned to hold an information meeting with residents in a format that would be decided after consultation with municipal authorities.

Some six months after construction began, Goodman held its first information sessions, which a few dozen Tsukuba residents attended over two evenings in August. The invitation-only meetings took place at a local restaurant and included a multi-course meal, according to four residents who attended.
"It felt like a hospitality event," one of the attendees said, asking to be identified only by her first name, Keiko, to protect her anonymity.
"I'm not against data centres in general, but if anything, the event made me feel distrustful of them."

Goodman said it is "committed to engaging with residents openly and respectfully, and we will continue to do so." It also said the company has "exceeded legal requirements and those set out in guidelines."

In guidelines published in May, the Japan Data Center Council, an industry body of which Goodman is a member, stressed the importance of consultation, saying operators should view engagement as "a forum for discussion and mutual understanding, not a one-sided report."
1b23457d728e6268: GEORGE TOWN: The High Court here has fixed tomorrow for the defence hearing of four men charged with murdering bullying victim T. Nhaveen.
Judge Datuk Mohd Radzi Abdul Hamid fixed the hearing after the defence sought an adjournment to allow both sides time to go through four finalised witness statements.
Maanveer Singh Dhillon told the court the defence had met the four men at the prison but had limited time with them during each session.
"We just finalised it, and the written statement is ready," he told the court.
Maanveer handed the four statements to the court and the prosecution, led by Deputy Public Prosecutor Mohd Amri Johari, during this morning's proceedings.
Amri told the court that the prosecution required time to go through the four statements.
Following the submissions, Radzi allowed the adjournment and fixed the matter for 9.30am.
The defence also informed the court that one of the four accused needed the assistance of a Tamil interpreter.
The four accused are J. Ragesuthan, 26, S. Gokulan, 26, and two others who were juveniles at the time of the incident.
They were previously ordered to enter their defence on a charge of murdering Nhaveen, who was 18 when he was allegedly assaulted in June 2017.
Nhaveen, a former student of St Xavier's Institution, was allegedly assaulted by a group of youths near a school in Jalan Kaki Bukit, Gelugor, on June 9, 2017.
He was then admitted to hospital and died several days later after suffering serious injuries.
The case attracted widespread public attention and renewed calls for stronger action against bullying.
Besides Amri, Deputy Public Prosecutor Yazid Mustaqim Roslan also prosecuted.
Also appearing for the defence were R. Thevan and Lim Sheng Zhe.
90b10c914c3aa52a: GEORGE TOWN: Pengerusi Pakatan Harapan (PH) Pulau Pinang, Chow Kon Yeow berkata mesyuarat kepimpinan negeri yang pada asalnya dijadualkan pada September ditangguhkan kerana ramai pemimpin mempunyai urusan yang tidak dapat dielakkan.

c31305129e882d35: SINGAPORE, Oct 7 — Singapore’s revised Primary 1 registration framework aims to widen access to popular primary schools from 2027, but some Members of Parliament (MPs) have questioned how the changes will affect families living near these schools and whether they will actually lead to greater social mixing.
MP Gho Sze Kee raised concerns in Parliament today about the impact of the changes on families in Mountbatten, saying she had “many upset parents” in the constituency.
She noted that Kong Hwa School, the only primary school in Mountbatten, is already “routinely oversubscribed”.

Gho said some children within the area have to consider neighbouring schools, four of which — Tanjong Katong Primary School, Tao Nan School, CHIJ (Katong) Primary School and Ngee Ann Primary School — are among the 12 schools that will come under the new two-track Phase 2C scheme.

Under this new scheme, 12 schools in areas with relatively low levels of public housing will split places equally between children living within 2km of the school and those living more than 2km away, with no further distance priority within each track.

“It is unconscionable that a child living a stone’s throw away from a school should be forced to travel to another primary school further away simply because the school next door is very popular,” Gho said.

Gho asked Education Minister Desmond Lee whether the Ministry of Education (MOE) had assessed where children who may no longer secure a place at these schools would go, as well as the distance and travel time they could face and the resulting pressure on neighbouring schools.

She also questioned whether using distance from a school was a reliable proxy for socio-economic diversity, pointing out that families living beyond 2km may not necessarily come from different socio-economic backgrounds than those living nearby.
“With this new framework, we are simply drawing a circle around a school and handicapping every child living within that circle,” Gho said.
“Worse, this framework makes the assumption that children living outside of that circle will be from different socio-economic backgrounds.”
Lee: Social mixing depends on parents’ choices
Responding to Gho’s concerns, Lee said the changes were intended to widen access for children from different backgrounds while maintaining opportunities for those living near the schools.

He said MOE introduced the two-track scheme because relying solely on home-school distance may not substantially broaden access in neighbourhoods where the housing profile is predominantly of one type.
However, he stressed that whether the changes ultimately result in greater social mixing would also depend on parents’ choices.

“We recognise the frustrations of parents who come to to us and say, ‘Well, I live opposite a school, but that’s a popular school, and alumni go in. There are siblings in there, you know, and I don’t get to go there,’” Lee said.
He said the changes are intended to broaden opportunities for access and give more families a chance to apply to popular schools.
Lee added that the 12 schools were selected because public housing makes up less than 40 per cent of dwelling units within a 2km radius of the school.

By setting aside places for children living beyond 2km, the scheme aims to broaden access and encourage a more diverse student mix, although Lee noted the outcome would ultimately depend on parents’ choices and other factors.
No fixed benchmark for ‘ideal’ social mix
NCMP Andre Low asked whether MOE would establish baseline indicators to measure socio-economic mixing and assess the outcomes of the two-track scheme.
Lee said there was no single benchmark for an “ideal” socio-economic mix because schools and neighbourhoods differ.
He added that MOE would monitor the socio-economic mix of schools, neighbourhood characteristics and broader trends as it reviews the implementation of the two-track system.
The system would also be “porous”, Lee said.
If places allocated to children living beyond 2km are not fully taken up, they can “flow back” to children living within 2km.
Parent volunteer scheme remains unchanged
There will also be no changes to the parent volunteer scheme, which provides an opportunity for parents to contribute to and get to know schools.
However, schools will continue to decide whether and how to implement the scheme based on their individual needs.

Lee said MOE had decided not to make structural changes to Phase 2A and Phase 2B for now, balancing the aim of widening access with recognising the contributions of alumni, school partners and community volunteers.
He added that there would also be no changes to the Phase 2A priority accorded to MOE Kindergarten pupils.
The revised Primary 1 registration framework will take effect from the 2027 Primary 1 registration exercise. — AsiaOne
5dc26d13ec452d8a: KUALA LUMPUR: Mall operators are urging the government to consider measures to ease rising operating costs for shopping malls, including extending electricity cost protection under the Automatic Fuel Adjustment (AFA) mechanism and reducing the Sales and Service Tax (SST).

Sunway Malls group managing director H.C. Chan, who is also an adviser to the Malaysia Shopping Malls Association, said electricity charges and SST were among the group's key wishlist items for the 2027 Budget, as higher operating costs continue to weigh on the retail industry.

Speaking to the media at the Sunway Ipoh Mall Key Tenant Unveiling, Chan said the government should consider extending electricity cost protection measures beyond households to shopping malls, given the significant amount of electricity required to operate large retail complexes.
"For us, we have a very short wishlist. One is electricity charges to operate the mall. We hope the government can consider shielding malls, not just houses.
"We must remember that there are a lot of purchases in Malaysia's shopping malls and a lot of money spent in shopping malls," he said.

Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim had previously said the government was exploring ways to make the tax system more progressive, including whether certain elements of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) could be incorporated into the existing SST framework.
Anwar said the SST would remain the basis of the current tax system, although selected GST features could be considered if they helped improve the system.

Chan said electricity was a significant operating cost for shopping malls, which require substantial power for air-conditioning, lighting, lifts, escalators, security systems and other common facilities.
He said measures to contain electricity costs would help mall operators manage expenses and reduce cost pressures across the wider retail ecosystem.
This would be particularly important as mall operators face rising operating costs while having to remain competitive in attracting retailers and maintaining consumer traffic, he added.
On SST, Chan called for the rate to be reduced, saying this could help ease pressure on both businesses and consumers.

"The SST was 8.0 per cent, and now it is 6.0 per cent. We hope the government will consider reducing the SST, perhaps by half from 6.0 per cent to 3.0 per cent for a certain period, to ease pressure on the market," he said.
Chan said a lower tax burden could give businesses greater room to manage costs while supporting consumer spending, particularly as households remain sensitive to the rising cost of living.
"You must remember that a significant amount of consumer spending in Malaysia takes place in shopping malls. Such a measure would help reduce the burden not only on the B40 but also the M40.
"Over the past six to nine months, the ongoing war and higher costs have put considerable pressure on consumer spending, particularly among the B40 and M40 segments.

"We therefore hope the government will consider halving the SST from 6.0 per cent to 3.0 per cent, while also maintaining support on electricity charges under the AFA mechanism for as long as possible. That would be our wishlist," he said.
cbf035e52cc6f083: SINGAPORE, Oct 7 — Barely a day after air quality improved slightly in northern and southern Singapore, the 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) in both regions returned to the unhealthy range.
The 24-hour PSI in northern and southern Singapore crossed into the unhealthy range at 11am.
By 1pm, all five regions recorded unhealthy PSI levels, ranging from 101 to 132.
Meanwhile, one-hour PM2.5 concentrations ranged from 65 to 126, with western Singapore recording the highest concentration reading of 126.
Concentration readings between 56 to 150µg/m3 dall within the elevated band.

The Republic’s 24-hour PSI forecast is expected to be in the high-moderate to mid-unhealthy range, according to the National Environment Agency’s daily haze situation update issued on Tuesday evening.

Neighbouring Malaysia is also experiencing deteriorating air quality. Data from the government’s Air Quality Index Management System at 1.30pm showed that 37 out of 68 monitoring stations recorded unhealthy air quality. — AsiaOne

f1edb418371b59c9: SEOUL, Oct 7 — South Korea’s president said today the country is taking steps to protect the country’s booming cultural cache, launching a new “K-brand” authentication system that will let consumers know if goods they are purchasing are the real deal.

Led by K-pop acts such as BTS, hit Netflix series Squid Game and KPop Demon Hunters, the so-called “Hallyu”, or Korean cultural wave, saw content exports hit a record US$14.9 billion (RM61 billion) last year, surpassing overseas sales of computers and home appliances.

The popularity of so-called K-food and K-beauty products, meanwhile, saw exports of agricultural and fisheries products and cosmetics hit record highs of US$12.4 billion and US$11.4 billion, respectively.

Under Seoul’s new “K-Brand Government Certification System”, consumers will now be able to check whether a product is authentic by scanning a QR code attached to it with their mobile phone, President Lee Jae Myung said today.
“From K-beauty and K-food to K-fashion, Korean brands are rapidly becoming part of the everyday lives of people around the world,” Lee said on X.
“But as K-brands grow in popularity, Korean companies are also suffering increasing damage from counterfeit products overseas,” he said.
“The government will respond swiftly to counterfeit products overseas,” Lee said, adding that it would “no longer leave our companies to fight alone”.
Thirty-one companies have already signed up for the scheme, including Samyang Foods, the maker of Buldak spicy chicken ramen, and Amorepacific, South Korea’s largest cosmetics company.
According to data released by the OECD in 2024, the global market for counterfeit “K-brand” products was approximately 11 trillion won.
The love of all things Korean has also impacted arrivals to the country, with the number of foreign tourists hitting an all-time high of 18.94 million last year. — AFP
b8398e04473191f1: KUALA LUMPUR: Ten former Negri Sembilan state executive councillors have filed an originating summons at the Seremban High Court challenging the validity of a gazette revoking their appointments.
Their lawyers, Hafarizam Wan & Aisha Mubarak, said in a statement that the suit was filed on Oct 5 against the state secretary and the state government.
The former councillors are challenging the validity of a Sept 24 state government gazette concerning the revocation of their appointments as members of the state executive council.
The law firm said the former councillors were seeking, among other things, a declaration on whether the gazette issued by the state secretary was valid and enforceable.
35763cba65b20119: PETALING JAYA: Daily use of multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) in Malaysia is projected to reach 43% by 2030, exceeding the global forecast of 30%, according to Ericsson ConsumerLab research.
Multimodal AI refers to systems that combine text, voice, images and video – technology that is expected to become increasingly integrated into consumers' daily lives.
The Ericsson ConsumerLab research was based on responses from over 43,000 smartphone users aged 15 to 69 across 27 markets, including Malaysia, Indonesia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand.
Ericsson Malaysia, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh head David Hagerbro said Malaysians are increasingly using AI in various aspects of their daily lives and expect it to work reliably wherever they are.
"Malaysia is well placed to respond to this shift, with a strong foundation already in place with Digital Nasional Bhd's (DNB) 5G network," he said in a statement.
Hagerbro said the network, built with Ericsson technology, offers advanced 5G capabilities and AI-based operations that can support the reliable connectivity required by emerging AI applications.
"DNB's 5G network enables mobile operators to offer connectivity tailored to different services, with more consistent performance and predictable response times as AI use grows," he said.
He said this could create opportunities for Malaysian developers and businesses to develop services that make AI more useful in everyday life and support the country’s digitalisation ambitions.

Globally, daily multimodal AI use is projected to rise from 10% currently to 30% by 2030. The increased use of images, video and voice is expected to generate more upload traffic and short bursts of demand, particularly in urban areas.
The research identified a group of AI "super users" who currently account for 35% of AI usage and are expected to account for more than 80% by 2030.
Their behaviour suggests that AI interactions will become more frequent and span multiple devices, increasing reliance on mobile connectivity.
The report also highlighted the expected growth of "agentic AI", which can perform tasks such as making bookings and managing schedules on behalf of users.
Across the markets surveyed, 38% of smartphone users expect to use agentic AI by 2030, up from 4% currently.
As these services can operate in the background, the report said they would increase demand for predictable network performance and secure connections.
Trust will also be important to adoption, with more than half of daily AI users expressing strong concerns about fake or compromised AI assistants.
0b5b296b1fe303b2: BUSAN, Oct 7 — Tan Sri Michelle Yeoh said she embraces new challenges and does not fear failure, as she returned to the Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) for the first time in 15 years to receive its Asian Filmmaker of the Year award.
The 64-year-old also appeared at the festival as the lead actor and producer of It’s My Time, which was invited to the event’s Gala Presentation section.
“Every day, when I wake up, I look forward to a new challenge in life and I think that is what life is about,” Yeoh said at a press conference, according to Yonhap.
“I am not afraid of failures. It is like a heartbeat, it goes up, it comes down,” she added.

Yeoh credited her willingness to pursue new opportunities with allowing her to take on diverse roles and collaborate with young directors, including Daniel Scheinert and Daniel Kwan on Everything Everywhere All at Once (2022), the film that earned her the Academy Award for Best Actress.
She said she was drawn to It’s My Time because of the challenge of portraying an old woman and conveying the message that new opportunities remain possible at any age.
In the film, Yeoh plays Zhao Yanhong, a nursing-home resident in her 70s who discovers a gift for solving the Rubik’s Cube.
The role draws inspiration from Zhao Wenying, a retired math teacher who became the quickest over-60 competitor to solve the puzzle blindfolded.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Malaysian actress Michelle Yeoh speaks during a press conference for her film ‘It’s My Time’ at the 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) at the Busan Cinema Center in Busan October 7, 2026. — AFP pic
Yeoh also produced the picture, which is directed by Bai Xue and marks her return to Chinese-language cinema.

Reflecting on her early Hollywood years, Yeoh said she was initially shocked at being labeled a “minority” and grew frustrated over being offered stereotypical roles for Asian women, such as working at a Korean restaurant or a Chinese laundromat, even after her breakthrough appearance in the James Bond film Tomorrow Never Dies (1997), Variety reports.
She waited roughly two years before taking on Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, a film that brought one of the harder moments of her career when she had knee surgery partway through the shoot.
Yeoh now laughs about the scene where Chow Yun-fat dies in her arms.
“If you pull back the camera, because I had knee surgery, I couldn’t cross legs and cradle Chow. I had my leg literally on a box,” she said, according to Variety.
“So it’s kind of funny looking, with one leg up there and then Chow up here.”

Winning Best Actress at the Oscars felt like a “dream,” Yeoh said, as she credited Korean actor Youn Yuh-jung, the first Asian to win Best Supporting Actress at the Academy Awards, with inspiring her.
“She opened the door for me to believe that it is a possibility,” Yeoh said, as she encouraged more Asian filmmakers and actors to continue telling their stories.

“The possibility is definitely there and we have to aspire to not just make it a one-off, because we have so many amazing stories to tell,” she added, citing Korean auteurs such as Lee Chang-dong, Park Chan-wook and Bong Joon-ho.
Yeoh said she looked forward to Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love and expressed a desire to work with Park Chan-wook and Bong Joon-ho.
“I hope I have the privilege of working more in Korea as well, because I’m a big fan of K-pop, K-drama, Korean food, and especially Korean movies,” she said.
When asked whether directing might be next, Yeoh ruled it out.
“I love being an actor; I actually love being a producer, but I think being an amazing, great director, you have no life,” she said.

“There is so much of your vision of that person, that writer, and I think I am not able to rise to that. So I will stick to what I know a little bit better, and hope to support directors who have that vision.”

Yeoh said she enjoys working with new and young directors, noting that the Daniels were only on their second film with Everything Everywhere All at Once, and that Roshan Sethi, who directed her latest film The Surgeon, which premiered at Toronto, is also a second-time director.
“If you read their script, you’d wonder if they were actually a little bit insane. The fact is they are, that’s why they’re such geniuses,” Yeoh said of the Daniels.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Malaysian actress Michelle Yeoh arrives on the red carpet during the opening ceremony of the 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) at the Busan Cinema Center in Busan October 6, 2026. — AFP pic
Yeoh has a long history with Busan, having taken part in the festival’s Pusan Promotion Plan as a producer in 2002 and attended in 2011 with The Lady.
Earlier in 2026, she received an honorary Golden Bear at the Berlin Film Festival.
Yeoh, whose acting career spans more than four decades, said cinema remains an indispensable part of her life.
“I think cinema is so very much part of my life that I don’t know what I would do without it,” she said.
She acknowledged the many distractions and platforms available to audiences today, but still touted the enduring power of cinema.
“I hope cinema will always be there because that is the moment that you have for yourself to be honest,” she said.

She added, “When you take that time to watch that one film, it is a choice of your own and for that two hours, you can shut out the rest of the world and give yourself those two hours to enjoy something that you have picked.”
Yeoh also reflected on her role as a bridge between East and West.

“I think I spent quite a few years trying to build a bridge from the East to the West, and then now from the West to the East,” she said. “And hopefully, the bridge will just stay there and I’m able to cross over whenever I want.”
6bdbad9b9d4cd985: GEORGE TOWN: The Penang Domestic Trade and Cost of Living Ministry has received 21 complaints over alleged fuel quality issues at several petrol stations in the northern region.
The complaints, which surfaced on social media, have been investigated by its Penang enforcement officers, who inspected both the affected petrol stations and complainants, including vehicle owners.

As part of the investigation, fuel samples were collected from both parties and sent to the Chemistry Department for analysis to determine whether they contained water, diesel or other substances that could affect fuel quality.
State director S. Jegan said no conclusion could yet be drawn on the cause or composition of the fuel until the laboratory results were available.

"At this stage, the ministry is still awaiting the analysis results from the Chemistry Department. Therefore, it is too early to make any conclusion regarding the cause or contents of the fuel," he said today.

Jegan said the ministry had taken note of the statements and commitments by the oil companies involved to cooperate fully with the authorities in addressing the issue and ensuring compliance with prescribed fuel specifications.
He said the ministry would continue monitoring developments and take appropriate action based on the investigation findings and Chemistry Department analysis.
The public experiencing fuel quality problems or having relevant information have also been advised to lodge complaints with Caltex and Petron to facilitate further inspections and investigations.

The ministry urged consumers not to draw premature conclusions based on information circulating on social media and to submit official complaints to the ministry through WhatsApp at 019-848 8000, the e-Aduan KPDN portal, its 1-800-886-800 call centre or the EzADU KPDN mobile application.
The ministry said consumer interests and safety would remain a priority, with action taken based on facts, investigation findings and technical evidence.
It was reported that the Penang chapter of the ministry had found no evidence of water contamination in RON95 storage tanks at a Batu Kawan petrol station following a viral complaint.
The inspections were conducted jointly with the oil company and station operator after a social media post alleged vehicle problems following refuelling recently.
367ff1ed6fb6c495: PETALING JAYA: Kerajaan gagal mengutip berbilion-bilion ringgit hutang, dengan hanya 5% daripada keseluruhan RM9.273 bilion hutang tertunggak berjaya dikutip tahun lalu, kata Ahli Parlimen Pasir Gudang Hassan Karim.

Ketika membahaskan laporan Ketua Audit Negara 2026 di Dewan Rakyat, Hassan berkata kelemahan kerajaan dalam mengutip hutang amat membimbangkan, memandangkan hutang persekutuan meningkat 5.9% tahun lalu kepada RM1.321 trilion.
“Kerajaan agak baik dalam membuat pinjaman tetapi tidak begitu baik dalam mengutip hutang,” katanya.
“Apa buktinya? Laporan Ketua Audit Negara menunjukkan berbilion-bilion ringgit hutang oleh pelbagai pihak kepada kerajaan persekutuan masih belum dibayar.
“Ada yang berhutang sehingga 40 tahun tanpa diselesaikan... Laporan itu mendedahkan bahawa sistem kutipan hutang kerajaan persekutuan gagal.”
Kenyataan Hassan itu dibuat isu hutang tertunggak yang belum dibayar kepada agensi kerajaan mendapat perhatian.

Pada Isnin, Zetrix AI Bhd, anak syarikat Kumpulan MYEG, berkata ia telah mengemukakan cadangan penyelesaian kepada kerajaan bagi menyelesaikan tunggakan hutang RM314 juta kepada Jabatan Pengangkutan Jalan (JPJ).

Menteri Pengangkutan Loke Siew Fook berkata tunggakan itu melibatkan fi dan saman yang dikutip syarikat berkenaan sejak Mei, sambil menambah bahawa kementerian dan JPJ akan menetapkan tarikh akhir untuk jumlah itu dijelaskan serta mengambil langkah sewajarnya bagi mendapatkan semula dana tersebut.

Hassan turut menggesa kerajaan supaya tidak menggunakan wang pembayar cukai untuk menyelamatkan syarikat berkaitan kerajaan atau firma swasta yang mengalami kerugian, memandangkan tahap hutang negara yang tinggi.

Merujuk kepada sebuah syarikat penerbangan nasional, Hassan berkata beliau dimaklumkan bahawa syarikat itu mempunyai hutang jangka pendek sebanyak RM18.4 bilion dan kerugian suku tahunan sebanyak RM830 juta.
Hassan berkata kerajaan harus menolak sebarang permintaan bantuan kewangan daripada syarikat berkenaan.
“Jika syarikat ini mengetuk pintu Kementerian Kewangan dan meminta bantuan, saya harap kerajaan menolaknya kerana kerajaan sendiri berhutang,” katanya.
“Kerajaan mempunyai perkara lain yang perlu diselesaikan.”
Bulan lalu, AirAsia menafikan bahawa syarikat itu ada meminta bantuan kerajaan.
Pengasas bersama dan penasihat Kumpulan AirAsia Tony Fernandes berkata operasi syarikat penerbangan itu kekal mampan dan ia tidak pernah meminta bantuan kerajaan sepanjang 25 tahun operasinya.

Beliau turut menafikan laporan bahawa kerajaan menghubungi syarikat penerbangan pesaing untuk mengambil alih sebahagian daripada laluan domestik AirAsia, dengan berkata Putrajaya telah mengesahkan kepadanya bahawa tiada perbincangan sedemikian berlaku.
06e411c9f7b690ca: GEORGE TOWN: Penang Pakatan Harapan (PH) chairman Chow Kon Yeow says a state chapter meeting initially scheduled for September has been postponed as many leaders have prior engagements.
"We are looking to hold the next meeting sometime in November," he told reporters here.

Penang PH deputy chairman Faiz Fadzil said last month that the Sept 26 meeting would discuss Umno's position in the state government following the party’s attacks against the coalition at the Umno general assembly.
Faiz later confirmed that the meeting had been postponed, but gave no reason.

On Sept 12, Permatang Pauh Umno chief Zaidi Said claimed at the general assembly that Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi's strategy of cooperating with PKR was aimed at weakening the party, which would eventually affect its coalition partner, DAP.
He said DAP, seen as Umno's "main enemy", could not be defeated directly because the party had its own voter base.
Zaidi later resigned as a Seberang Perai city councillor and apologised for his speech.
When asked if Zaidi's remarks and subsequent resignation would be discussed at the meeting, Chow said such issues "would be taken up".
257fc80cc477ba4f: KOTA KINABALU: The mother of the late Zara Qairina Mahathir knew that her daughter had tried vaping.
Noraidah Lamat, 46, told Coroner Amir Shah Amir Hassan that she had asked Zara about vaping after learning that some male pupils had brought vapes to school.
"I asked Zara about the matter and whether she was involved. At first, she said no, but when I asked her again, Zara admitted that she had tried it a little.
"From there, I knew that Zara had tried vaping," Noraidah said.
Under examination-in-chief by counsel Shahlan Jufri, Noraidah, the 82nd deponent, said she was initially not angry when questioning Zara.
However, she became slightly angry after her daughter admitted that she had tried vaping.
"I asked her why she had followed the others. I told her she was lucky she had not been called up at school," she said.
Noraidah said she advised Zara about the harmful effects of vaping and told her not to try it again.
She said she did not punish Zara over the incident but had nagged her about the harmful effects of vaping.
Asked whether she had verbally abused or hit Zara over the matter, Noraidah said she had not.
Asked by Shahlan how Zara reacted at the time, Noraidah said her daughter chuckled, perhaps because she did not yet understand the harmful effects of vaping.
She said Zara and her friends might have been merely curious to try it.
Noraidah said Zara would return to normal after being reprimanded, even if she initially sulked or became upset.
"If she sulked or became angry, the longest it would last was about 30 minutes. After that, our relationship would return to normal as usual," she said.
Noraidah said Zara would then talk to her as usual, including asking whether they could go out or whether there was anything to eat at home.
She also testified that after the incident, she never again became aware of Zara trying or using a vape.
"After that incident, I never knew of it happening again, nor did I hear anything about it from her friends," she said.
In response to another question by Shahlan, Noraidah testified that Zara had been consistent from the beginning about her ambition to become a policewoman.
"I don't know why she wanted to become a policewoman, but I thought perhaps it was because police officers wear uniforms and Zara was also an active person," Noraidah said.
